entities.name: Marcus Porcius Cato Licinianus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Marcus Porcius Cato Licinianus (died 151 BCE) was a distinguished Roman jurist and military officer, best known as the elder son of the formidable statesman Cato the Elder and his first wife, Licinia. His premature death at a pivotal moment in the Roman Republic's expansion denied Rome a potentially influential political and intellectual figure, whose legal acumen and adherence to traditional Roman values, inherited from his censorious father, positioned him as a guardian of civic order and probity. His life, though cut short, illuminates the intellectual and moral currents within the Roman elite during the mid-2nd century BCE, a period marked by increasing Hellenistic influence and internal social strains.

Cato Licinianus received an exceptional education, personally overseen by his father, which encompassed rhetoric, military training, and a deep immersion in Roman law. He served with distinction in the Roman military, notably under Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus during the Third Macedonian War, participating in the decisive Battle of Pydna in 168 BCE, where he was severely wounded but displayed remarkable courage. Upon his return to Rome, he dedicated himself to the study and practice of law, quickly gaining renown for his expertise in civil law (ius civile) and his eloquent advocacy. His legal writings, though largely lost to antiquity, were highly regarded by subsequent Roman jurists, including Cicero, for their clarity and adherence to foundational Roman legal principles.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Marcus Porcius Cato Licinianus was a significant Roman jurist whose legal scholarship, though largely lost, influenced the development of Roman civil law and was highly regarded by later legal minds like Cicero. His early death prevented a potentially impactful political career during a crucial period of the Roman Republic.
